content:
Multiple Dropbox users have received emails from the cloud storage service informing them that their accounts were accessed without authorisation, constituting a security breach. The latest reports indicate that around 5,000 accounts were affected, with files from approximately 1,500 of those accounts being downloaded.

The root cause of the issue appears to be that Dropbox failed to perform identity verification when an attacker set up a single sign-on option through a third-party company…

Developer Yoni Levy shared a copy of the email he received on X.

Other Dropbox users reported receiving the same email, in which the company attributed the incident to a problem with the single sign-on (SSO) option using Lenovo account IDs.

Dropbox, however, claimed the flaw lay in Lenovo's email verification process, but The Cybersec Guru pointed out that the bigger issue seems to be that Dropbox itself did not require users to authenticate through their existing login method when adding a new SSO.

  • Reconnaissance and filtering: The attacker collects target email addresses (from leaked databases, LinkedIn, customer lists, etc. — email addresses are essentially public information).
  • Malicious IdP registration: The attacker registers a Lenovo ID using victim@example.com. Because Lenovo's verification step is absent or can be bypassed, there is no need to access the victim's mailbox. The display name is set to something disposable — one of the victims who recovered their hijacked account found it set to "John Madden," the late NFL announcer, which is clearly indicative of large-scale, low-cost registrations.
  • Federated login: The attacker clicks "Continue with Lenovo account" on Dropbox. Lenovo's authorisation server issues a token, and its email claim matches the victim's Dropbox account.
  • Implicit account linking: Dropbox maps the email claim to an existing account and establishes a login session. No password is required, no additional verification is needed, and there is no "Do you want to link this new identity?" confirmation prompt. From Dropbox's perspective, a trusted IdP has vouched for that email address.

9to5Mac commentary

Although Lenovo's side did indeed fail in verifying email addresses, had Dropbox authenticated before allowing the newly linked ID to log in, the incident itself would not have caused any damage. Failing to do so is a serious oversight.

Dropbox has fixed the vulnerability and invalidated all sessions that were previously "authenticated" via Lenovo IDs.

If you have not yet enabled two-factor authentication for Dropbox, it is strongly recommended that you set it up immediately.
